short_claim: Givers and recipients agree only moderately on whether a supportive act occurred (kappa about .39)
source: Coriell, M., & Cohen, S. (1995). Concordance in the face of a stressful event: When do members of a dyad agree that one person supported the other? Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 69(2), 289-299.

design: Single-occasion dyadic comparison of independent retrospective checklists after an exam (student-reported received vs supporter-reported provided), within-dyad Cohen's kappa averaged across dyads; correlational predictors of concordance; no manipulation
population: 297 US undergraduate-supporter dyads at Carnegie Mellon (eight intro psychology classes; supporters were self-chosen close friends or roommates; students 57% men, median age 18; 99 man-man, 71 woman-woman, 127 mixed dyads); 220 dyads for competence and communality analyses; collection year not stated

short_claim: Invisible support (reported by provider, not recipient) predicts better adjustment; visible support does not
source: Bolger, N., Zuckerman, A., & Kessler, R. C. (2000). Invisible support and adjustment to stress. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 79(6), 953-961.

short_claim: Experiments: visible support is ineffective or raises distress by signalling inefficacy, while invisible support helps
source: Bolger, N., & Amarel, D. (2007). Effects of social support visibility on adjustment to stress: Experimental evidence. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 92(3), 458-475.
sections_read: Author-posted PDF of the published article (columbia.edu/~nb2229), pp. 458-473: abstract, introduction, Studies 1-3 Method and Results (Tables 1-5, Figures 2-3), mediation analyses, General Discussion, Unresolved Issues, Conclusions
design: Three randomised laboratory experiments; anticipated-speech stressor; scripted support from a female confederate peer delivered directly (visible) or as a question to the experimenter (invisible); Study 2 added no-support control; Study 3 five-cell incomplete factorial separating visibility, recipient-inefficacy and peer-inefficacy messages and content, with measured mediators
population: Female NYU introductory-psychology students; analysed n = 31, 86 and 150 (sum 267; abstract reports N = 257); female stranger confederates; years not stated
measured: Change in self-reported distress (6-9 POMS anxiety, depression and anger items, 0-10 scale) from baseline to just before an expected speech that was never given; manipulation checks; perceived supportiveness; reflected appraisal of inefficacy; upward social comparison
key_result: Invisible vs visible: Study 1 d = 1.09 (CI 0.37-1.81), p = .004; Study 2 d = 0.63 (CI 0.12-1.15), p = .017. Invisible vs none: Study 2 d = 0.36, p = .159; Study 3 d = 0.37 (CI -0.03 to 0.76), p = .069 (both n.s.). Visible vs none: Study 2 d = 0.27, p = .287 (n.s.); Study 3 visible support stating the recipient needed help raised distress 1.09 units (CI 0.43-1.75), d = 0.66, p = .001, and removing that message eliminated the harm. Reflected appraisal of inefficacy mediated about 45% of that effect; advice content showed no effect (p = .673)
evidence_grade: Moderate or mixed (causal within a lab analogue; one laboratory, women, strangers); Preliminary for invisible support beating no support; Theoretical for close relationships

recommended_change: Rewrite 03:31: in three lab experiments with female US undergraduates supported by a female stranger (analysed n = 31, 86, 150; abstract N = 257), indirect support produced smaller rises in anticipatory distress than direct support; its advantage over no support was not statistically significant; direct support raised distress only when it conveyed that the recipient needed help, partly via feeling seen as inefficacious. design: Cross-sectional survey of college students in 11 countries
population: College students from secondary population centres in India, Pakistan, Thailand, Mexico, Brazil, Japan, Hong Kong, the Philippines, Australia, England and the US; N not in abstract
measured: Rated importance of love for establishing, maintaining and dissolving marriage
key_result: Love rated most important in Western and Westernized nations and least in the nations the 1995 abstract calls 'underdeveloped Eastern'; differences larger for establishing marriage; few sex differences; greater importance in individualistic cultures; correlated with higher living standards, higher marriage and divorce rates, lower fertility. No percentages in abstract.
evidence_grade: Not used in paper; qualitative pattern Moderate among students; percentages unverified
recommended_change: None (not cited in paper chapters, README, CORRECTIONS or bibliography). If added later, cite only the qualitative student-sample pattern, avoid the dated 'underdeveloped Eastern' framing, and do not cite country percentages until the primary is read.
